name: Japanese 人工リーフ (artificial reef) submerged breakwater programme
place: Multiple sites nationwide (documented examples: Niigata Coast; Sugihama Coast, Mihama-cho, Fukui; Iburi Coast, Tomakomai/Shiraoi, Hokkaido)
type: submerged breakwater (wide-crested, trapezoidal rubble-mound), programme/class not a single site
purpose: coastal protection (storm-surge and wave protection, beach-erosion control); secondary aesthetic goal of preserving sea view vs. an emergent breakwater
year_built: ongoing, decades-old practice; Niigata's reef+breakwater programme active since ~FY1977 [R3]; national policy formalised by the 1999 Coastal Law revision [R1]
status: ongoing nationwide practice; Iburi Coast example re-evaluated and continuing as of the FY2022/Jan-2023 national public-works review [R9]

dimensions.crest_width_m: defining threshold ≥30-50m distinguishes 'artificial reef' from plain submerged breakwater [R6]; worked design examples cite 50m (block-covered) and 124m (breakwater-block) [R12]; another source gives 40-60m typical [R13]
dimensions.cross_section: trapezoidal, natural stone/crushed rock with armor layer, historically concrete blocks [R1][R2][R6]

cost: no programme-wide national total found; Iburi Coast example (bundled with seawalls, not reef alone): construction ¥148.8bn + maintenance ¥0.25bn ≈ ¥149.1bn total (FY2022 evaluation), roughly USD 1.0bn at ~¥150/USD (rough 2023 conversion, labelled) [R9]
designer: no single designer; JSCE design guidance and a national ministerial technical-standards ordinance (2004, Heisei 16) govern the type [R1][R8]
contractor: not applicable at programme level; Iburi Coast example executed directly by Hokkaido Development Bureau (MLIT) [R9]
financed_by: national government via MLIT public-works budget (直轄事業 / directly-managed project funding, cost-shared with affected prefecture) [R9]
motivation: 1999 Coastal Law revision shifted national policy from single emergent seawalls ('linear defense') to submerged wide-crested reef + sloped seawall ('areal defense'), explicitly to reduce overtopping/erosion while preserving the sea view [R1][R2]; Niigata driver was direct: ~350m max shoreline retreat since the Meiji era from river management + port development + Sea-of-Japan storms [R7]
outcome: Iburi Coast FY2022 national evaluation states the artificial reef stabilised beach topography and regenerated the sand beach (official quoted finding) [R9]; Niigata's programme credited by a local civil-engineering society with 'beach recovery' [R3]; a 1989 JSCE paper's existence indicates subsidence was serious enough at Niigata reefs to warrant a dedicated study, though its findings were not accessed [R15]
